questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly defines the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) in NIST SP 800-207's Zero Trust Architecture, as distinguished from the Policy Engine and the Policy Administrator?
options: The gatekeeper component that sits on the data path between subject and resource, enabling, monitoring, and terminating the connection based on what the Policy Administrator tells it to do
The component that runs the trust algorithm and outputs a grant, deny, or revoke decision for a given subject/resource pair
The component that establishes or shuts down the communication path and generates the session-specific credential the subject will use
A Continuous Diagnostics and Mitigation (CDM) system that reports asset state into the trust algorithm
The grouping of the Policy Engine and Policy Administrator together, described as the architecture's 'brain'
A SIEM pipeline that feeds activity logs into the Policy Engine's decision
questions.explain: The PEP is the gatekeeper that both the subject and the resource communicate through — it enables, monitors, and terminates the connection, but it never decides anything itself. The decision is made upstream by the Policy Engine, and the Policy Administrator is what acts on that decision by establishing the session and issuing the credential; the PEP only carries out what the PDP already decided.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C describes the Policy Administrator, not the PEP — the PA is the component that establishes or shuts down the communication path and issues the session-specific credential. The PEP is a distinct, separate component that sits on the data path and enforces what the PA already told it to do; confusing 'the thing that issues the credential' with 'the thing that enforces the connection' is exactly the mix-up Lesson 3 is built to prevent.

questions.prompt: Match each Zero Trust Architecture component from Lessons 3-4 to what it actually does.
right: Runs the trust algorithm and outputs a grant, deny, or revoke decision for a subject/resource pair
Establishes or shuts down the communication path and issues the session-specific credential
The gatekeeper on the data path that enables, monitors, and terminates the connection
NIST's grouping of the Policy Engine and Policy Administrator together as the architecture's 'brain'
questions.explain: The PE decides, the PA acts on that decision by establishing the session and issuing the credential, and the PEP is the separate gatekeeper sitting on the data path that actually enforces it. NIST groups the PE and PA together as the Policy Decision Point — the 'brain' — while the PEP stands apart as the 'gate.'

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the industry term for the breakdown of a single enforceable network boundary, driven by cloud adoption and remote access, is called ________.
questions.explain: De-perimeterization is Lesson 1's name for exactly what broke the castle-and-moat model: once resources, users, and devices no longer sit neatly inside one network boundary, there's no single enforceable perimeter left to defend, which is the gap NIST SP 800-207 was written to close.

questions.prompt: An admin spots a compromised account in the sign-in logs and disables it immediately. The attacker already holds a valid Microsoft Graph access token issued ten minutes earlier. Per Lesson 6, what happens to that token if Continuous Access Evaluation is enabled versus if it isn't?
options: With CAE enabled, Entra ID pushes the disablement event to Microsoft Graph and the token is revoked within minutes; without CAE, Graph keeps honoring the token until it naturally expires
With or without CAE, the token is revoked instantly, because disabling the account always invalidates every issued token immediately regardless of any additional mechanism
CAE only affects sign-in risk scoring, not already-issued access tokens, so the outcome is identical whether or not CAE is enabled
Without CAE the token is revoked instantly, while CAE actually delays revocation in order to batch multiple critical events together
questions.explain: This is the exact scenario Lesson 6 uses to motivate CAE: without it, a resource provider has no way to know the account status changed and keeps honoring the token for its full lifetime, commonly on the order of an hour. With CAE enabled, Entra ID pushes the account-disabled event to the CAE-enabled resource provider in near-real time, so the token is revoked within a few minutes instead of being honored until it naturally expires.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about device-related signals in a Conditional Access decision, per Lesson 7.
options: "Require Hybrid Azure AD joined device" and "Require device to be marked as compliant" are two distinct grant controls answering different questions
Intune evaluates a device against compliance rules on a recurring basis and reports a simple compliant/not-compliant state to Microsoft Entra ID
A device can be hybrid Azure AD joined without currently being compliant — for example, if disk encryption was disabled after the device was provisioned
Device compliance only needs to be checked once, at enrollment, since Intune policy almost never changes afterward
The granular compliance rules themselves live inside Microsoft Entra ID, with Intune only acting as a reporting dashboard
questions.explain: Hybrid Azure AD joined is about device provenance (where it came from and who provisioned it), while compliant is about present-day security posture — they're genuinely different signals, and a device can be hybrid-joined but no longer compliant if something like disk encryption gets disabled later. Intune evaluates compliance on a recurring basis and reports only the resulting state to Entra ID; the granular rules live in Intune, not Entra ID, and compliance has to be checked at the moment of the access decision, not just once at enrollment.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: on the AWS side of the identity fabric in Lesson 8, a federated identity receives short-lived, expiring temporary credentials tied to an assumed role, issued by AWS ________.
questions.explain: AWS Security Token Service (STS) issues the short-lived, expiring temporary credentials tied to an assumed role once a federated identity lands in AWS through IAM Identity Center — the same time-boxed, borrowed-privilege philosophy as PIM's eligible/activate/expire model on the Azure side.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a single access request into AWS, per Lesson 8's identity fabric, in the correct order.
items: User signs in once through Microsoft Entra ID, subject to Conditional Access
Entra ID evaluates device compliance and risk signals as part of the same sign-in
The authenticated identity federates over SAML into AWS IAM Identity Center
IAM Identity Center maps the identity to a permission set
AWS STS issues short-lived, expiring temporary credentials tied to an assumed role
questions.explain: Because Entra ID is the single identity source of truth, the sign-in itself — including device compliance and risk evaluation — happens before anything crosses into AWS. Only an already-verified identity federates over SAML into IAM Identity Center, which maps it to a permission set; AWS STS then issues the actual short-lived credentials the user works with, mirroring PIM's time-boxed elevation on the Azure side.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly defines micro-segmentation, as distinguished from ordinary network-tier segmentation (subnets, NSGs, hub-spoke)?
options: Writing enforcement policy at the level of an individual workload, attached to a workload identity rather than an IP address, instead of at the subnet or tier boundary
Dividing a network into a web tier, an app tier, and a data tier, with an NSG controlling traffic at each tier's boundary
Routing all traffic through a single central firewall so that every tier is forced to pass through one choke point
Assigning one shared NSG rule that allows every service inside a subnet to talk to every other service in that same subnet
Replacing a VPN with a site-to-site connection between two data centers
Encrypting all east-west traffic with TLS regardless of which specific workloads are communicating
questions.explain: Micro-segmentation shrinks the policy unit from a subnet or tier down to an individual workload, and attaches that policy to a workload identity — a certificate, a signed label, a tag — rather than to an IP address, so the policy travels with the workload even as it's rescheduled onto new hosts. That's a different, narrower unit of enforcement than a tier boundary.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes ordinary network-tier segmentation — exactly the thing Lesson 9 contrasts micro-segmentation against. A web/app/data tier split with an NSG at each boundary still leaves every one of the dozens of services inside one tier free to reach each other; that gap, inside the tier, is precisely what micro-segmentation closes by shrinking the policy unit down to the single workload.

questions.prompt: A contractor needs access to exactly one internal line-of-business app for a short-term project. Per Lesson 10, what's the key structural difference between granting that access via a traditional VPN versus via a ZTNA/software-defined-perimeter broker?
options: The VPN places the contractor's device onto the corporate network with broad reachability; the SDP broker evaluates identity and device posture first and opens a connection to only that one application, with no inbound port ever exposed
The VPN and the SDP broker both grant identical network-wide reachability, differing only in which encryption cipher is used
The SDP broker requires opening an inbound firewall port on the private network, while the VPN does not
The VPN authenticates per individual application request, while the SDP broker authenticates only once at connection time
questions.explain: A VPN's job ends at 'let this device onto the network,' after which network reachability — not the VPN — decides what the contractor can touch, almost always granting more than the one app they actually need. An SDP broker inverts that: it evaluates identity and device posture first, then opens a connection scoped to exactly the one authorized application, using an outbound-only connector that never opens an inbound port at all.

questions.prompt: Match each enterprise-scale PAM term from Lesson 11 to what it actually is.
right: A central inventory of every privileged role across an enterprise's systems, with a consistent definition of what each grants
The principle that certain role combinations should never be held by the same person because together they enable fraud or error
An emergency credential that bypasses the normal JIT approval chain, vaulted and alerted on separately
One consistent set of time-boxing, approval, and review rules applied across many underlying systems
questions.explain: A role catalog is what makes a consistent definition of 'privileged' possible across the whole enterprise, which is what lets segregation-of-duties conflicts actually be detected. Break-glass accounts deliberately sit outside that normal flow, governed instead by separate vaulting and mandatory after-action review. The enterprise-scale PAM policy is the one consistent rule set applied across every underlying system, even though the mechanics differ by system.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Microsoft's AD tiering model and Privileged Access Workstations, per Lesson 12.
options: A hard rule of AD tiering is that a credential valid at one tier is never allowed to log on to a system at a more sensitive tier
Tier 0 covers domain controllers and the identity infrastructure that controls everything else
A Privileged Access Workstation is used only for Tier 0 administration, with no email or general web browsing on it
AD tiering alone, with no additional device-level control, is fully sufficient to prevent credential theft
A help desk technician's Tier 2 workstation-admin credential is expected to also work for logging on to a domain controller
questions.explain: AD tiering's core rule is that a credential never crosses upward between tiers — Tier 0 is domain controllers and identity infrastructure, and a Tier 2 workstation-admin credential should never work on a Tier 0 system. But tiering only works if a Tier 0 credential is never typed on a lower-trust machine, which is exactly the gap a PAW closes: a hardened, single-purpose machine used only for Tier 0 work, since policy alone can't stop a compromised workstation from harvesting a credential the instant it's entered.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: ________ is the maximum scope of damage possible if one specific credential, device, or resource is compromised — independent of how likely that compromise actually is.
questions.explain: Lesson 14 is explicit that blast radius is a structural fact about the system, not a likelihood estimate — this service account can reach these resources, this role can write to this storage account — and that's exactly what makes it something an architecture review can pin down in writing before approval, rather than guess at.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about lateral-movement techniques and their countermeasures, per Lesson 15.
options: Pass-the-hash works because many authentication protocols accept a cached credential hash itself as proof of identity
Unique per-machine local administrator passwords make a hash dumped from one machine worthless against every other machine
Token/ticket theft sidesteps MFA because the stolen token is proof that MFA already happened at login, not a fresh check
Continuous Access Evaluation helps counter token theft by revoking tokens the moment a relevant signal changes, instead of honoring them for their full lifetime
Requiring MFA everywhere is, by itself, sufficient to stop pass-the-hash, token theft, and shared-credential abuse all at once
questions.explain: Pass-the-hash exploits protocols that accept a cached hash as identity proof, and unique per-machine admin passwords directly neutralize it by making a dumped hash worthless elsewhere. Token theft sidesteps MFA because the token itself is the proof MFA happened, not a fresh check — which is exactly why CAE's near-real-time revocation helps. Lesson 15's closing point is explicit that no single control, including MFA, stops all of these techniques at once; each needs a control matched specifically to it.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 16, a SOAR platform flags a single end-user workstation with high-confidence EDR malware indicators, and separately flags a production database server showing anomalous access patterns. Which design decision correctly applies Lesson 16's tiered automated-response pattern?
options: Auto-isolate the single workstation without waiting for approval, but route the production database server action to a human for approval before anything irreversible happens
Auto-isolate both resources immediately without human approval, since both detections came from the same SOAR platform
Require human approval for both detections, since any automated action always carries some risk of being wrong
Auto-isolate the database server immediately because production systems are more urgent, but require approval before isolating the workstation
questions.explain: Lesson 16's dividing line is blast radius, not detection confidence. Isolating one end-user workstation is a low-blast-radius action — worst case, one employee loses access briefly — so it's safe to auto-contain. Isolating a production database server is high-blast-radius: a false positive there creates an outage that looks like the incident it was meant to prevent, so it has to wait for a human to approve, even though the detection itself might be just as confident.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 14, put these steps of estimating a credential's blast radius during an architecture review in the order the lesson presents them.
items: Trace identity reach: what the IAM role or RBAC assignment actually permits, not what it was intended for
Trace network reach: what the device or workload can connect to over the network
Trace detection time: how long it would take anyone to notice abnormal behavior from this credential or device
Document the estimate in writing as part of the design, including whether the reach is actually required
questions.explain: Lesson 14 names identity reach, network reach, and detection time, in that order, as the three dimensions to trace because they don't move together — a role can be tightly scoped while the network path is wide open, or vice versa. The estimate only does its job once it's written down and attached to the design, with an honest answer about whether the reach is actually required for the stated purpose.

questions.prompt: Which of the following correctly defines Mutual TLS (mTLS), as distinguished from ordinary TLS?
options: A TLS handshake in which both the client and the server present and verify certificates, so each side cryptographically proves its identity to the other
A TLS handshake in which only the server presents a certificate, and the client remains anonymous at the transport layer
A protocol for issuing short-lived OAuth2 access tokens scoped to a specific operation
A technique for rotating a static API key automatically on a fixed schedule
A method for encrypting data at rest using a managed key service
A load-balancing technique that distributes service-to-service calls across multiple sidecar proxies
questions.explain: Mutual TLS flips ordinary TLS's one-sided proof: each side presents a certificate, and each side verifies the other's certificate before the connection is considered established. For service-to-service traffic, that means Service A can't connect to Service B at all unless it can cryptographically prove its own identity — there's no step where B just takes A's word for it.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes ordinary TLS, not mutual TLS — ordinary TLS only proves the server's identity to the client, leaving the client anonymous at the transport layer. Mutual TLS is specifically the addition of a second, reciprocal proof: the client also presents and the server also verifies a certificate, which is the exact capability a static API key never provided.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about workload identity for CI/CD and automation, per Lesson 19.
options: A managed identity is assigned directly to a cloud resource by the platform itself, with no credential a human or script ever sees or stores
OIDC federation lets a CI/CD pipeline exchange a short-lived token its own platform already issues for a short-lived cloud credential, with no stored secret involved
A long-lived pipeline secret sitting in a CI/CD platform's secrets store is typically narrowly scoped and automatically rotated every few minutes
Both managed identity and OIDC federation replace a shared secret with a federated trust relationship verified cryptographically on every request
Managed identity fully solves the authentication problem for a CI/CD pipeline that runs entirely on infrastructure the CI/CD vendor controls
questions.explain: Managed identity eliminates the credential entirely for a resource the cloud platform itself hosts, and OIDC federation extends that same no-stored-secret benefit to a pipeline running on vendor-controlled infrastructure by trusting a token the CI/CD platform already issues. A long-lived pipeline secret is the opposite of narrowly scoped and frequently rotated — it's exactly the high-value, rarely-rotated target Lesson 19 warns about — and managed identity specifically does not solve the vendor-infrastructure case, which is precisely why OIDC federation exists as a separate mechanism.

questions.prompt: Match each SaaS-security term from Lesson 20 to what it actually is.
right: SaaS applications adopted by employees or departments without IT provisioning or visibility
A proxy or API-based control point that extends DLP and conditional-access-style policy to apps you don't host
Continuous scanning of a connected SaaS tenant's own configuration for misconfigurations like open sharing links or missing MFA
The approval an employee grants a third-party app to access their data, creating a long-lived integration that needs its own governance
questions.explain: Shadow IT is the unmanaged layer most SaaS security programs start by discovering. A CASB sits on the path to a SaaS app and enforces DLP- and conditional-access-style policy there. SSPM instead looks inward at the app's own configuration for drift a CASB would never see. OAuth app consent is a separate governance concern entirely — a long-lived, often invisible integration created the moment someone clicks 'Allow.'

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: machine-readable classification metadata attached to a file or email — which a mail gateway, cloud app, or DLP engine inspects before acting — is called a ________.
questions.explain: A sensitivity label is what turns 'this contains sensitive data' from a statement in a policy document into an attribute every downstream enforcement point can actually act on — blocking external forwarding, blocking public link sharing, or flagging a copy to removable media.

questions.prompt: An organization reports a single blended figure: '92% MFA coverage across the company.' Per Lesson 23, what's the specific problem with reporting MFA coverage this way?
options: A blended figure can hide that every admin account, or every service/non-human identity, is still on a phishable factor while standard users pulled the average up
MFA coverage should never be measured as a percentage, only as a raw count of enrolled users
92% is mathematically impossible to achieve with phishing-resistant MFA, so the number must be measuring something else entirely
Blended metrics are always an outcome metric, so by definition they overstate real risk reduction rather than hiding anything
questions.explain: Lesson 23 names this exact failure mode: report phishing-resistant MFA coverage by population — admin accounts, standard users, service/non-human identities — separately, because a blended '92% MFA coverage' figure can hide that the highest-value accounts are still on a phishable factor while a large population of lower-risk users carries the average up.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the CISA Zero Trust Maturity Model, per Lesson 21.
options: The model scores five pillars separately rather than producing one overall combined score
Visibility & Analytics, Automation & Orchestration, and Governance are cross-cutting capabilities that span all five pillars rather than belonging to any single one
The four maturity stages are Traditional, Initial, Advanced, and Optimal, applied consistently to every pillar and capability
An organization with excellent micro-segmentation but no governance process for approving new segmentation rules is automatically scored as mature by the model
The jump from Advanced to Optimal reduces real-world risk more fundamentally than the jump from Traditional through Initial to Advanced
questions.explain: CISA's model deliberately scores five pillars separately, because averaging would hide exactly the gap an attacker would exploit, and layers three cross-cutting capabilities across all of them. A pillar can look technically advanced and still fail on governance — the model is built to catch exactly that, not wave it through. And Lesson 21 is explicit that most of the actual risk reduction happens in the Traditional-to-Advanced climb, not in the later Advanced-to-Optimal jump, which mainly buys speed and scale.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the outcome metric that measures how long it takes monitoring to flag a credential or host moving from one system to the next is abbreviated ________.
acceptedAnswers: mean time to detect lateral movement
questions.explain: Mean time to detect (MTTD) lateral movement is, per Lesson 23, one of the cleanest single proof points that zero trust changed real exposure, because it measures the thing an attacker needs most directly: time. Before micro-segmentation and identity-aware logging it's often measured in days; after, in minutes.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 22's scoring process, put these steps of honestly scoring one pillar against the CISA maturity model in the correct order.
items: Pick one pillar at a time instead of scoring all five simultaneously
Start from the Optimal stage definition and ask whether it's true everywhere, continuously
Drop down a stage at a time until the honest answer to that stage's definition is genuinely yes
Score to the evidence you can point to in production, not to a plan or a purchased capability
Record the specific coverage gap, not just the final stage label
questions.explain: Lesson 22's process works backward from the top: pick one pillar so evidence doesn't blur together, start at Optimal and drop down until you hit a stage that's honestly true today, score only to production evidence rather than plans or tool capability, and finally write down the specific gap — because the gap, not the label alone, is what tells the next person what actually needs fixing.

questions.prompt: Per Lesson 26, a gap involving a shared service account with no expiration sits directly in front of production customer data, and fixing it is entirely within the security team's own control. A second, headline-grabbing vulnerability class sits behind three other controls and would require three other teams to migrate first. Which gap should be prioritized first, and why?
options: The shared service account: it scores high on both risk (direct exposure to production data) and feasibility (fixable within the team's own control) — the quadrant Lesson 26 says to fix first
The headline vulnerability: anything that sounds alarming in the news should always be fixed first, regardless of feasibility
Neither: gaps should always be fixed in the order they were originally discovered, not prioritized by risk or feasibility
The headline vulnerability: feasibility doesn't matter, only risk, so the hardest-sounding problem always goes first
questions.explain: Lesson 26's quadrant explicitly warns that a gap can sound alarming in marketing or the news while sitting behind several other controls, scoring lower in real risk than it sounds — and a gap that sounds boring, like an unexpired shared service account in front of production data, can score higher. High risk plus high feasibility is the quadrant to fix first; scoring on risk or feasibility alone produces a worse roadmap than scoring both together.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement that is a sign of 'zero trust theater,' per Lesson 28.
options: A conditional access product is licensed and turned on, but every existing access path is added to an allow-list so the net effect on real access is close to zero
A segmentation policy is written but deployed in report-only mode and never flipped to actually block anything
A roadmap item is closed because the project plan says it's done, without checking whether the thing it was supposed to fix is actually fixed
A segmentation project ships covering only the two easiest systems and is reported as 'segmentation implemented' without qualification
Comparing the access path that existed before an initiative to the access path that exists after it is itself a sign of zero trust theater
questions.explain: All four of the first patterns are the specific signs Lesson 28 names: a control licensed but allow-listed into irrelevance, a policy left permanently in report-only mode, success measured by what shipped rather than what changed, and scope narrowed until the control was easy rather than complete. The before/after access-path comparison is the opposite of theater — it's the exact test Lesson 28 says every initiative has to pass to prove it wasn't theater.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: per Lesson 26, a known, documented, low-risk, low-feasibility gap that is explicitly deferred in writing, with a stated reason, is called a ________ gap.
questions.explain: A parked gap is explicitly deferred, in writing, with a reason — 'we're not fixing this now because X' is a defensible answer, which is different from a gap that's silently never gotten to and quietly forgotten.

questions.code:
route: /patients/{id}/claims
requireWorkloadIdentity: true
allowedCallers:
  - service: analytics-platform
    maxTokenLifetime: 15m
  - service: claimflow-integration
    maxTokenLifetime: 15m
    scopes: ["claims:submit"]
denyIfNoToken: true
questions.prompt: In the MediCore API gateway policy above, from Lesson 29, the `claimflow-integration` caller is scoped to exactly `claims:submit` with a 15-minute token lifetime. What zero-trust principle does this specific design choice enforce for ClaimFlow's service-to-service access?
options: Least-privilege, short-lived workload identity: the caller can do only the one action it needs, and any leaked token is useful for only a narrow window
Network segmentation: the policy controls which subnet ClaimFlow's traffic is routed through
Device compliance: the policy checks whether ClaimFlow's calling device meets Intune's compliance rules
Continuous Access Evaluation: the policy pushes critical events like account disablement to the API gateway in real time
questions.explain: Scoping the caller to exactly `claims:submit` — never broader than the one action it performs — and expiring its token in 15 minutes is least-privilege and short-lived workload identity applied to a service-to-service call, replacing the long-lived, broadly-scoped static credential pattern Lesson 18 and 19 warned against. It's exactly the design decision Lesson 31's case study comes back to, because the old SFTP integration it was replacing had neither property.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 30's scorecard, Meridian's Networks and Applications & Workloads pillars target a jump from Traditional to Advanced, but the Data pillar stays at Initial even after Lesson 29's full design. Per Lesson 30, why?
options: Lesson 29 classified PHI as sensitive but hadn't yet built the enforcement — DLP, encryption-at-rest audits, access tied to classification — that actually acts on that classification everywhere it lives
Data was never addressed anywhere in Lesson 29's design, so no progress was possible to score at all
The CISA model doesn't allow the Data pillar to advance past Initial for any healthcare organization
Scoring was deliberately averaged down across all five pillars to make the overall maturity percentage look more conservative
questions.explain: Lesson 30 is explicit that Lesson 29's design classified PHI in MediCore and the AWS analytics platform, but classification alone isn't enforcement — the DLP, encryption audits, and classification-driven access reviews that would actually act on that classification everywhere PHI lives hadn't been built yet, which is exactly why Data stays at Initial while Networks and Applications & Workloads can target Advanced.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about what went wrong in the Meridian case study, per Lesson 31.
options: The legacy SFTP batch export was formally excluded from the audit's scope, pending a decommission expected within two quarters
The `svc-claimflow-sftp` service account had read access to the entire shared folder structure, not just the claims files ClaimFlow actually needed
The Conditional Access policy from Lesson 29 already covered the scheduled, non-interactive SFTP job, so MFA should have blocked the credential-stuffing attempt
The decommission date slipping by four months automatically triggered a re-review of the exclusion before the next audit cycle
The account was compromised through a reused password discovered via credential stuffing against ClaimFlow's own corporate email, not through a flaw in Meridian's Conditional Access policy itself
questions.explain: The SFTP export was a formally documented, reasonable-at-the-time scope exclusion, and the service account behind it was over-scoped to the entire shared folder rather than just the claims files. Conditional Access from Lesson 29 applied to interactive sign-ins, not the scheduled, non-interactive SFTP job, so it never covered that credential at all. And critically, nothing re-triggered a review when the decommission date slipped — the exclusion quietly outlived its own deadline. The actual breach came from a reused password found via credential stuffing against ClaimFlow's own email, not a failure in Meridian's Conditional Access policy.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Lesson 29's zero trust architecture design for Meridian Health Partners in the order they were actually performed.
items: Make Microsoft Entra ID the single policy decision point for every sign-in, on-prem or cloud
Replace the flat on-prem network with four named micro-segments reached only through a broker
Design for assume-breach: block direct workstation-to-workstation protocols across segment boundaries and define an automated containment playbook
Classify PHI and wrap MediCore behind an API gateway requiring short-lived workload identity tokens for every service-to-service call
questions.explain: Lesson 29 builds the architecture in exactly this dependency order: identity first (Steps 1-2), because segmentation decisions need identity signals to key off of; then network segmentation (Steps 3-4), replacing the flat network with named segments and a broker; then assume-breach containment (Steps 5-6), designed on top of that segmentation; and finally data and application controls (Steps 7-8), which assume the segmentation layer already exists to contain what happens if they fail.
